knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of system-form selection based on symbolic factor patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symbolic factor pattern is determined by a matrix sparsity pattern and a chosen ordering, not by numerical values. For a positive-definite normal equation factored without pivoting, it fixes the structural Cholesky pattern up to numerical cancellation. For an indefinite augmented system, value-dependent stability pivoting may permute or delay pivots and create factor structure not predicted by a fixed symmetric ordering. Thus a lower symbolic-fill estimate does not by itself certify lower realized memory or work across system forms; selection must retain numerical-stability admissibility and permit rejection, reselection, or fallback after factorization diagnostics.

Fill-Sensitive System Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic-cost rule for choosing among equivalent Newton-system formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given algebraically equivalent Newton systems \(M_qz_q=r_q\) indexed by \(q\in Q\), construct each structural graph, choose an admissible ordering \(P_q\), and symbolically predict the factor pattern \(\widehat L_q\). Assign \(C_q=\alpha\,\operatorname{nnz}(\widehat L_q)+\beta\sum_k \widehat c_{qk}^{\,2}\), where \(\widehat c_{qk}\) is the predicted frontal-column size and \(\alpha,\beta>0\). Discard any form failing prescribed dimension, memory, or stability constraints, select \(q_*\in\operatorname*{argmin} C_q\), numerically factor \(P_{q_*}M_{q_*}P_{q_*}^{\mathsf T}\), and recover the full Newton direction by the corresponding elimination identities. If no form is admissible, report failure rather than factorizing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predict factor fill for each equivalent Newton system, reject inadmissible forms, and factor the feasible form with the lowest estimated storage and arithmetic cost.

knowledge_statements.title: System-Form Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-number amplification caused by forming primal normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \(D\succ0\) be diagonal. With \(B=AD^{1/2}\), the primal normal-equation matrix is \(N=ADA^{\mathsf T}=BB^{\mathsf T}\). Its eigenvalues are the squared singular values of \(B\); hence \(\kappa_2(N)=\kappa_2(B)^2\). Therefore eliminating to normal equations squares the spectral condition number of the scaled constraint operator. A system-form comparison must consequently account for both the conditioning of the retained matrix and the stability of the eliminations used to recover omitted Newton variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal equations square the spectral condition number of the scaled constraint matrix, so a smaller system can be substantially harder to solve accurately.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank.
\(D\succ0\) is diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(ADA^{\mathsf T})=\kappa_2(AD^{1/2})^2\).

assumptions_latex: \(D\succ0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^{-1}\widehat{\Delta x}-A^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\Delta y}-g=0,\qquad A\widehat{\Delta x}-h=-\rho.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual correspondence between a weighted normal equation and its recovered two-block system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(D^{-1}\Delta x-A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y=g\) and \(A\Delta x=h\), with \(D\succ0\). Let \(N=ADA^{\mathsf T}\), let \(\widehat{\Delta y}\) approximately solve \(N\Delta y=h-ADg\), and recover \(\widehat{\Delta x}=D(g+A^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\Delta y})\) in exact arithmetic. Then the first block residual is zero and \(A\widehat{\Delta x}-h=-\rho\), where \(\rho=(h-ADg)-N\widehat{\Delta y}\). Thus the reduced residual exactly certifies the residual of the recovered block equations, but does not bound forward error for ill-conditioned \(N\) or include rounding in recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With exact recovery, the normal-equation residual is exactly the remaining residual of the original block system. A small residual still need not imply an accurate direction for an ill-conditioned matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Transfer for an Eliminated Normal Equation
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Transfer for an Eliminated Normal Equation
Numerical Stability Exposure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-error exposure of normal-equation and indefinite-system solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a backward-stable linear solver applied to a nonsingular matrix \(M\) returns \(\widehat z\) satisfying \((M+E)\widehat z=r\) with \(\lVert E\rVert_2\le\eta\lVert M\rVert_2\). If \(\eta\kappa_2(M)<1\), then the relative forward error is bounded by \(\lVert\widehat z-z\rVert_2/\lVert z\rVert_2\le \eta\kappa_2(M)/(1-\eta\kappa_2(M))\). For \(M=BB^{\mathsf T}\), this exposure depends on \(\kappa_2(B)^2\). Thus forming normal equations can lose roughly twice as many conditioning-related digits as solving a suitably scaled formulation whose conditioning is proportional to \(\kappa_2(B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward stability does not prevent large forward error: normal equations expose the solve to the squared condition number of the scaled constraint matrix.

The computed solution satisfies the stated normwise backward-error model.
\(\eta\kappa_2(M)<1\).

children.title: Scaling Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning response under diagonal row and column scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be nonsingular and let \(R\) and \(C\) be nonsingular diagonal scaling matrices. For \(\widetilde B=RBC\), the transformed system \(\widetilde B\widetilde z=Rr\), followed by \(z=C\widetilde z\), is algebraically equivalent to \(Bz=r\). Its spectral condition number satisfies \(\kappa_2(\widetilde B)\le\kappa_2(R)\kappa_2(B)\kappa_2(C)\) and \(\kappa_2(\widetilde B)\ge\kappa_2(B)/(\kappa_2(R)\kappa_2(C))\). Hence diagonal scaling preserves the exact solution after variable recovery but may improve or worsen finite-precision sensitivity by factors governed by the scaling condition numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal scaling preserves the exact system after recovery, but it can materially improve or worsen the condition number seen by a numerical solver.
assumptions_latex: \(B\), \(R\), and \(C\) are nonsingular.
\(R\) and \(C\) are diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(B)/(\kappa_2(R)\kappa_2(C))\le\kappa_2(RBC)\le\kappa_2(R)\kappa_2(B)\kappa_2(C)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic equivalence and two-sided condition-number bounds are correct, but the record supplies no authoritative scaling reference with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: \(N\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto the null space of \(N\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit behavior of positive diagonal regularization for a symmetric positive-semidefinite system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\succeq0\), let \(P_0\) be the spectral projector onto \(\ker N\), and set \(y_\delta=(N+\delta I)^{-1}r\) for \(\delta>0\). As \(\delta\downarrow0\), \(y_\delta=N^\dagger(I-P_0)r+\delta^{-1}P_0r+o(1)\). If \(r\in\operatorname{range}(N)\), then \(y_\delta\to N^\dagger r\), the minimum-norm solution of \(Ny=r\). If \(P_0r\ne0\), then \(\|y_\delta\|_2\ge\|P_0r\|_2/\delta\), so the regularized solutions diverge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularization converges to the minimum-norm solution for a compatible singular system, but amplifies an incompatible null-space component like one over the regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Regularization Limit
Regularization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias and residual introduced by positive diagonal regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\succ0\), \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(y=N^{-1}r\), and \(y_\delta=(N+\delta I)^{-1}r\) for \(\delta>0\). Then \(y_\delta-y=-\delta(N+\delta I)^{-1}y\), so \(\lVert y_\delta-y\rVert_2\le \delta\lVert y\rVert_2/(\lambda_{\min}(N)+\delta)\). Moreover, the residual in the unregularized equation is \(Ny_\delta-r=-\delta y_\delta\). Regularization raises the smallest eigenvalue and improves \(\kappa_2(N+\delta I)=(\lambda_{\max}(N)+\delta)/(\lambda_{\min}(N)+\delta)\), but introduces a quantifiable perturbation in both the solution and original residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive regularization improves an SPD system's conditioning while introducing bounded solution bias and a residual equal to minus the regularization times the computed vector.
assumptions_latex: \(N\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert y_\delta-y\rVert_2\le\delta\lVert y\rVert_2/(\lambda_{\min}(N)+\delta)\) and \(Ny_\delta-r=-\delta y_\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SPD regularization identities, bias bound, residual identity, and condition-number expression are consistent, but no supporting regularization locator is cited.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\succ0\) and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\succ0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |e_{s,i}|\le\frac{|e_{c,i}|+s_i|e_{x,i}|}{x_i},\quad\text{with the symmetric bound for recovery through }s_i^{-1}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise sensitivity of complementarity-direction recovery when a primal coordinate or slack approaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a strictly positive primal-dual iterate, \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=r_c\) gives \(\Delta s_i=(r_{c,i}-s_i\Delta x_i)/x_i\). If \(r_{c,i}\) and \(\Delta x_i\) are perturbed by \(e_{c,i}\) and \(e_{x,i}\), the recovered error is \(e_{s,i}=(e_{c,i}-s_i e_{x,i})/x_i\), so \(|e_{s,i}|\le (|e_{c,i}|+s_i|e_{x,i}|)/x_i\). Recovery is therefore arbitrarily sensitive along a sequence with \(x_i\downarrow0\) unless the numerator errors decrease proportionally. Recovering \(\Delta x_i\) by division by \(s_i\) has the symmetric boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovering an eliminated complementarity direction requires division by a primal coordinate or slack. A denominator approaching zero can strongly amplify otherwise small residual and direction errors.
knowledge_statements.title: Late-Iteration Complementarity-Recovery Amplification
Late-Iteration Stability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-path scaling degeneracy near a strictly complementary LP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Along an exact central path satisfying \(x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu\), define \(D(\mu)=X(\mu)S(\mu)^{-1}\). Suppose the limiting solution is strictly complementary and contains indices \(i,j\) with \(x_i^*>0\) and \(s_j^*>0\). Then \(d_i(\mu)=\Theta(\mu^{-1})\), whereas \(d_j(\mu)=\Theta(\mu)\); consequently \(\max_k d_k(\mu)/\min_k d_k(\mu)=\Omega(\mu^{-2})\). Thus the diagonal scaling and associated normal equations may become severely ill-conditioned late in the iteration even though every \(x(\mu)\) and \(s(\mu)\) remains strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a mixed strictly complementary solution, central-path scaling entries separate like inverse mu and mu, producing a spread of at least order inverse mu squared.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i(\mu)s_i(\mu)=\mu\) with \(x(\mu),s(\mu)>0\).
The limit is strictly complementary.
Both a positive primal component and a positive dual-slack component occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_k d_k(\mu)/\min_k d_k(\mu)=\Omega(\mu^{-2})\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymptotic scaling follows under convergence to the stated strictly complementary limit, but this specialized failure-boundary claim needs a source specifically supporting the central-path asymptotics. The inventory's generic limit-point entries are not attached to the record.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-wise selection among algebraically equivalent barrier Newton-system forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(Q\) be a finite set of system forms that recover the same exact Newton direction. For each \(q\in Q\), estimate its factorization cost, memory demand, and numerical-stability risk. Exclude forms violating prescribed resource or stability limits. If the current form remains admissible, retain it unless another admissible form exceeds a prescribed switching-benefit threshold; otherwise select an admissible form immediately. Solve the selected system, recover every eliminated component, and accept the direction only when its residuals in the original KKT equations meet the prescribed tolerances. If no form is admissible or validation fails, invoke the prescribed regularization or higher-stability fallback and report numerical failure if that fallback fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose among equivalent Newton systems using current cost, memory, and stability estimates, apply hysteresis to avoid marginal switches, and accept a recovered direction only after validation in the original KKT equations.
assumptions_latex: The candidate forms recover the same exact Newton direction whenever their required eliminations are valid.
Resource limits, stability limits, switching thresholds, residual tolerances, and fallback rules are specified.
Cost, memory, and stability estimates are available at the selection point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns an original-KKT-residual-accepted direction from an admissible form, or an explicit numerical-failure report after its prescribed fallback fails.

notation.meaning: Finite set of candidate Newton-system forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Validated Adaptive System-Form Selection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of predicted savings in adaptive system-form switching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A predicted reduction in factorization cost does not imply a reduction in total solve time when symbolic analysis, matrix formation, data conversion, refactorization, or cache disruption caused by switching exceeds the predicted saving. Noisy or stale estimates can also alternate the selected form between iterations. Consequently, a switching policy requires overhead-aware estimates or hysteresis; original-KKT residual validation checks the computed direction but does not certify that the selected form was the cheapest or that switching improved total complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switching can lose overall when its overhead exceeds predicted savings, and inaccurate estimates can cause oscillation; residual validation protects direction quality, not performance optimality.
assumptions_latex: System-form changes may incur nonzero formation, symbolic-analysis, conversion, refactorization, or memory-hierarchy costs.
Selection estimates may differ from realized costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual acceptance does not imply performance dominance, and benefit thresholds must account for switching overhead and estimation error.
knowledge_statements.title: Switching-Overhead and Estimator-Error Boundary
Adaptive System-Form Switching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-wise switching among equivalent barrier Newton systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(Q\) index equivalent Newton-system forms. For each \(q\in Q\), estimate factorization cost \(C_q^k\), memory \(M_q^k\), and stability indicator \(S_q^k\), and define \(Q_k=\{q\in Q:M_q^k\le M_{\max},\ S_q^k\le S_{\max}\}\). If \(Q_k=\varnothing\), invoke a prescribed regularization fallback and recompute admissibility, or report numerical failure. If \(Q_k\ne\varnothing\) and the current form \(q_{k-1}\notin Q_k\), select a form in \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in Q_k}C_q^k\). If \(q_{k-1}\in Q_k\), retain it unless some \(q\in Q_k\) satisfies \(C_q^k\le(1-\tau)C_{q_{k-1}}^k\), in which case select a minimum-cost form among those satisfying this inequality. Solve the selected system, recover the common Newton direction, and accept it only if it passes residual tests in the original KKT equations; otherwise invoke the prescribed fallback or report numerical failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the current Newton-system form remains admissible, switch only when predicted savings exceed the hysteresis threshold. If it becomes inadmissible, choose an admissible form immediately. Accept the recovered direction only after original-KKT residual tests.
assumptions_latex: Candidate forms recover the same exact Newton direction.
Cost, memory, and stability estimates are available.
\(0<\tau<1\), admissibility thresholds, residual tolerances, and fallback rules are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a residual-accepted Newton direction obtained from a form in \(Q_k\), or an explicit numerical-failure report after the prescribed fallback fails.

notation.meaning: predicted cost of form q at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination-tree representation of dependencies implied by a filled Cholesky graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Number vertices by elimination order. For each vertex \(j\), define \(\operatorname{parent}(j)\) as its smallest-indexed neighbor \(i>j\) in the filled graph, leaving \(j\) a root if no such neighbor exists. These arcs form the elimination forest. Every later vertex \(i>j\) with a structural factor entry \(L_{ij}\) is an ancestor of \(j\), exposing independent subtrees until their dependency paths merge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first later filled neighbor is a vertex's elimination-tree parent, and every later factor neighbor is an ancestor.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chordal-completion and zero-fill characterization of symbolic elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The filled graph \(G_\pi^+\) produced by symbolic elimination is chordal, and \(\pi\) is a perfect elimination ordering of that filled graph: each vertex's later neighbors form a clique. No fill is introduced, \(E_\pi^+=E_0\), exactly when \(\pi\) is already a perfect elimination ordering of \(G_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symbolic elimination creates a chordal completion; an ordering is zero-fill exactly when it is a perfect elimination ordering of the original graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Filled Graph and Perfect Elimination
Elimination-Structure Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation of symbolic Cholesky elimination and fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite with structural graph \(G_0=(V,E_0)\), and let \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) be an elimination ordering. Immediately before eliminating \(v_k\), connect every pair of its remaining neighbors and then remove \(v_k\). The union of the original and inserted edges is the filled graph \(G_\pi^+=(V,E_\pi^+)\). In exact symbolic Cholesky analysis without numerical cancellation, an off-diagonal entry is structurally present in the permuted triangular factor exactly when its corresponding oriented edge belongs to \(E_\pi^+\). Together with the diagonal entries, these oriented edges determine the symbolic factor pattern, storage, and column counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an SPD matrix, symbolic elimination makes each eliminated vertex's remaining neighbors a clique. The resulting filled graph determines the structural nonzeros of the permuted Cholesky factor.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
\(G_0\) is the symmetric structural graph of \(M\).
\(\pi\) is a permutation of the vertices.
Numerical cancellation is ignored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symbolic pattern of the permuted Cholesky factor consists of its diagonal and the oriented edges of \(G_\pi^+\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-degree variant using inexpensive degree estimates on the evolving filled graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an inexpensive estimate or bound \(\widetilde d(v)\) for the exact degree \(d_G(v)\) of every active vertex in the current elimination graph. Select a vertex minimizing \(\widetilde d(v)\), eliminate it, update the quotient representation, and recompute affected estimates. Because \(\widetilde d(v)\) need not equal \(d_G(v)\), the selected vertex need not have exact minimum current degree; the result is an approximate minimum-degree ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate minimum degree selects vertices using cheaply maintained estimates of current filled degrees.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case limitation of explicit and implicit minimum-degree implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elimination graph can contain a clique on \(\Theta(n)\) active vertices. Explicit fill storage may therefore require \(\Theta(n^2)\) adjacency entries, and no minimum-degree tie rule guarantees sparse factors on arbitrary graphs. Quotient graphs and approximate degrees reduce update work on favorable instances but do not remove this worst-case dense-fill boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-degree heuristics and quotient representations cannot prevent quadratic active structure when elimination creates a large clique.

Duplicate active neighbors are removed when a degree is evaluated.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit representation of eliminated cliques used by practical minimum-degree methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent an eliminated clique by an element node adjacent to its still-active boundary instead of explicitly inserting every clique edge. For an active vertex \(v\), its filled neighborhood is obtained from its adjacent active vertices and the active boundaries of its incident elements, with duplicates removed. This quotient representation determines the same active adjacency relation as explicit fill materialization while supporting degree estimation and indistinguishable-vertex merging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotient graphs encode eliminated cliques as elements and recover filled neighborhoods from their active boundaries.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Graph Degree Representation
Minimum-Degree Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimum-degree heuristic on the evolving elimination graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected structural graph \(G_0=(V,E_0)\), initialize \(G\leftarrow G_0\) and an empty ordering \(\pi\). While vertices remain, choose a vertex \(v\) of minimum current degree in \(G\), breaking ties by a fixed rule; append \(v\) to \(\pi\), add all missing edges among the current neighbors of \(v\), and delete \(v\) and its incident edges. Return \(\pi\). The degree used at every step is the degree in the updated elimination graph, not the original graph. The algorithm is a fill-reduction heuristic and does not generally guarantee a globally minimum-fill ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly eliminate a current minimum-degree vertex, clique its remaining neighbors, and update degrees; the resulting ordering heuristically reduces fill without guaranteeing optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(G_0\) is a finite undirected graph.
A deterministic tie-breaking rule is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(\pi\) is a permutation generated by minimum current degree under successive fill updates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly describes exact minimum degree on the evolving filled graph and properly disclaims global minimum-fill optimality, but it has no cited source with an inspectable locator.

Every vertex in each \(V_i\) precedes every vertex in \(S\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Freedom to order distinct components at one nested-dissection split.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a vertex separator and let \(V_1,\ldots,V_t\) be the components of \(G-S\). Concatenate arbitrary internal orderings of the \(V_i\), in any component order, and then all vertices of \(S\). Elimination before reaching \(S\) creates no fill edge between distinct \(V_i\) and \(V_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated components may be ordered in any order before their separator without creating cross-component fill.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Component Ordering Freedom
Nested-Dissection Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive separator-based ordering for sparse symmetric factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), choose a vertex separator \(S\subset V\) such that the components \(V_1,\ldots,V_t\) of \(G-S\) are suitably balanced. Recursively compute nested-dissection orderings \(\pi_i\) for each induced graph \(G[V_i]\), and return the concatenation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_t,\pi_S)\), where \(\pi_S\) is any selected ordering of the separator. Recursion stops on components below a prescribed size, which are ordered by a base method. Consequently, every component interior is eliminated before the separator coupling it to other components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively separate the graph into balanced components, order each component first, and place its separator last so cross-component coupling is postponed.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
A separator routine and base-case ordering are specified.
Each recursive separator yields strictly smaller subproblems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every recursive split, all vertices of each \(V_i\) precede all vertices of \(S\) in \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: component vertex sets after separator removal

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive separator-last algorithm is correctly scoped and its content kind fits the terminal container, but no nested-dissection source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Graph Separator Structure
children.top_down_role: Separator organization relevant to elimination trees and frontal matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Separator Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex separators and balance for elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A vertex-separator decomposition is a partition \(V=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_t\), where \(t\ge2\), every \(V_i\) is nonempty, and no edge joins \(V_i\) to \(V_j\) for distinct \(i,j\). The set \(S\) is the vertex separator. For \(0<\alpha<1\), the decomposition is \(\alpha\)-balanced when \(|V_i|\le\alpha|V|\) for every \(i\). Equivalently, every path joining vertices in distinct sets \(V_i\) and \(V_j\) meets \(S\). The separator size is \(|S|\); its size and the balance of the separated parts govern its usefulness in recursive elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced vertex separator is a vertex set whose removal leaves at least two nonempty, mutually disconnected parts, none containing more than a fixed fraction of all vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The separator decomposition is \(\alpha\)-balanced exactly when \(|V_i|\le\alpha|V|\) for every separated part \(V_i\).

children.title: Separator Quality Effects
children.top_down_role: Fill, work, and parallelism consequences of separator balance or size.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized multifrontal costs induced by a balanced recursive separator hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an \(n\)-vertex subproblem is divided into children of sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_t\), and its separator contributes a dense front of order at most \(c\,s(n)\). In the stated idealized model, nested-dissection factorization satisfies \(M(n)\le\sum_iM(n_i)+O(s(n)^2)\) for factor storage and \(W(n)\le\sum_iW(n_i)+O(s(n)^3)\) for arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each separator contributes quadratic storage and cubic dense-front work, yielding recursive hierarchy cost bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Hierarchy Work and Storage Recurrences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every recursive subproblem of size \(m\) has at most a fixed number of children whose total size is at most \(m\), every child has size at most \(\beta m\) for fixed \(\beta<1\), and the separator size is \(s(m)=O(\sqrt m)\), then the separator recurrences yield \(M(n)=O(n\log n)\) and \(W(n)=O(n^{3/2})\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of unbalanced separators on recursion depth and available hierarchy parallelism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every child of an \(m\)-vertex recursive split has size at most \(\beta m\) for one fixed \(\beta<1\), the separator hierarchy has depth \(O(\log n)\). A separator may be small yet leave a child of size \(m-O(1)\); repeated splits of this kind can produce depth \(\Theta(n)\), invalidating logarithmic-depth and associated parallelism claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small separators alone do not ensure a shallow hierarchy; uniform balance is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balance Requirement for Logarithmic Hierarchy Depth
knowledge_statements.title: Balance Requirement for Logarithmic Hierarchy Depth
Separator Quality Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of balanced graph separators on fill in a nested-dissection elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be the structural graph of a symmetric sparse matrix, and let \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\mathbin{\dot\cup}S\), where no edge joins \(V_1\) to \(V_2\). If every vertex of \(V_1\cup V_2\) is eliminated before the separator \(S\), elimination creates no fill edge joining a remaining vertex of \(V_1\) to one of \(V_2\). Fill generated through either component is confined to that component together with \(S\), while vertices of \(S\) may become mutually adjacent. Consequently, smaller balanced separators bound the sizes of separator fronts and generally reduce symbolic fill and factorization work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating separated components before their separator localizes fill; smaller balanced separators therefore produce smaller fronts and usually less storage and arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the structural graph of a symmetric matrix.
\(S\) separates \(V_1\) from \(V_2\).
Vertices in \(V_1\cup V_2\) precede vertices in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{\mathrm{fill}}\cap(V_1\times V_2)=\varnothing\), and separator size controls the associated frontal dimensions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard elimination-graph property of nested dissection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fill-localization claim fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but the asserted effect of separator size on fronts, fill, and work needs a specific nested-dissection or sparse-elimination source locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition required for quotient-graph balance to represent fine-vertex balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each quotient vertex \(i\) the aggregate weight \(w_i=|A_i|\). If every component \(C_r\) of \(Q-C\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in C_r}w_i\le\beta\sum_iw_i\), then its lifted fine region contains at most \(\beta|V|\) vertices. Balance measured only by the number of quotient vertices has no such implication when aggregate sizes vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted coarse balance transfers to fine-level vertex balance; unweighted coarse balance can fail for unequal aggregates.

If \(C\subseteq V(Q)\) separates quotient vertex sets \(I\) and \(J\), then \(S=\bigcup_{i\in C}A_i\) separates \(U_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\) from \(U_J=\bigcup_{j\in J}A_j\) in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of aggregates represented by a coarse separator separates the corresponding fine-level regions.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifting a Quotient-Graph Separator
Multilevel Ordering Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic multilevel separator ordering for a symmetric sparse matrix graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G_0=(V_0,E_0)\), a minimum coarse size \(n_c\), and a balance tolerance \(\beta\in[1/2,1)\). Construct successively coarser graphs \(G_0,G_1,\ldots,G_q\) by aggregating vertices until \(|V_q|\le n_c\). Compute on \(G_q\) a separator whose removal leaves parts of size at most \(\beta|V_q|\); project the partition back through the levels and refine each projected separator locally. Recursively order each separated subgraph first and its refined separator last. Stop recursion at the prescribed leaf size and output the concatenated vertex permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coarsen the graph, find and refine a balanced separator while uncoarsening, then recursively order subdomains before separators.
assumptions_latex: \(G_0\) is finite and undirected.
Each coarse vertex represents a disjoint aggregate of finer vertices.
The separator routine satisfies the chosen balance tolerance \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output permutation orders every recursive component before its separating vertex set.

notation.meaning: maximum permitted fraction in either separated part

Adding a structural nonzero, changing the permutation, or applying unmodeled value-dependent delayed pivots may create fill outside the allocation and requires symbolic extension or reanalysis. If the new structural pattern is a subpattern of the old one and the other assumptions remain fixed, the old allocation remains a conservative upper bound.

Symbolic-Structure Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse across barrier iterations having a fixed structural sparsity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A^{(k)}\) be symmetric matrices with identical structural nonzero pattern, and fix a permutation matrix \(P\). Symbolic elimination applied to \(P^{T}A^{(k)}P\) produces the same elimination tree, column counts, and allocated factor pattern for every \(k\), provided structural zeros are retained and the numeric factorization uses no value-dependent pivoting. Thus the ordering, elimination tree, supernode partition, and factor-storage layout may be computed once and reused; only numeric factor entries must be recomputed. Accidental numerical cancellation may remove entries but does not invalidate the symbolic upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed sparsity pattern and fixed non-pivoting ordering permit reuse of the elimination tree, predicted fill, supernodes, and storage layout.

A supernodal variant groups columns with compatible filled structure and performs the same operations with dense triangular-solve and matrix-update kernels. In exact arithmetic both compute the unique positive-diagonal \(L\) satisfying \(B=LL^T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each elimination-tree node, multifrontal Cholesky assembles a dense front from original entries and child contributions, factors its fully summed pivot block, and passes the remaining Schur-complement contribution to its parent. Processing all fronts produces the positive-diagonal sparse factor \(L\) satisfying \(B=LL^T\) in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multifrontal Cholesky assembles dense fronts, eliminates completed pivots, and passes Schur-complement contributions up the elimination tree.

This is a backward-error statement and does not imply small forward error for ill-conditioned \(B\).

Numeric Cholesky Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left-looking scalar Cholesky under a precomputed sparse ordering and pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), a permutation \(P\), and an allocated lower-triangular symbolic pattern. Set \(B=P^{T}AP\). For \(j=1,\ldots,n\), compute \(d_j=B_{jj}-\sum_{k<j}L_{jk}^{2}\), set \(L_{jj}=\sqrt{d_j}\), and, for each allocated index \(i>j\), set \(L_{ij}=(B_{ij}-\sum_{k<j}L_{ik}L_{jk})/L_{jj}\), with sums restricted to stored intersections. On successful completion output \(L\); solve systems by triangular substitutions using \(P^{T}AP=LL^{T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the symbolic pattern, compute each positive diagonal and its lower-column entries, yielding a sparse Cholesky factor for triangular solves.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a permutation matrix.
The allocated pattern contains every structural Cholesky entry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{T}AP=LL^{T}\), where \(L\) is lower triangular with \(L_{jj}>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cholesky Factorization of a Reordered Positive-Definite Normal-Equation Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numeric Cholesky factorization and its trailing-submatrix update for a symmetrically reordered interior-point normal-equation matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=P(AD^2A^T)P^T\), where \(P\) is an \(m\times m\) permutation matrix. Assume that \(A\) has full row rank and that \(M\succ0\). The Cholesky algorithm computes the unique lower-triangular matrix \(L\) with positive diagonal entries such that \(LL^T=M\). At step \(i\), it sets \(L_{ii}=\sqrt{M_{ii}}\), sets \(L_{ji}=M_{ji}/L_{ii}\) for \(j=i+1,\ldots,m\), and performs the trailing update \(M_{i+1:m,i+1:m}\leftarrow M_{i+1:m,i+1:m}-M_{i+1:m,i}M_{i+1:m,i}^T/M_{ii}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated symmetrically reordered normal-equation matrix, assuming full row rank of A and positive definiteness of M, Cholesky factorization computes the unique lower-triangular factor L with positive diagonal satisfying LLᵀ = M. Each pivot step forms one column of L and applies a rank-one update to the trailing submatrix.
assumptions_latex: M=P(AD^2A^T)P^T
P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\text{ is a permutation matrix}
\operatorname{rank}(A)=m
M\succ0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,L\text{ lower triangular with }L_{ii}>0\text{ and }LL^T=M,\text{ and the stated pivot and trailing updates compute }L.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) elimination step, let \(d_j^{\mathrm{raw}}=a_{jj}^{(j)}\) be the current scalar pivot and let \(\eta_j>0\) be a prescribed floor. Set \(d_j=\max\{d_j^{\mathrm{raw}},\eta_j\}\), form the multipliers with \(d_j\), and continue the Schur-complement updates. The resulting factors satisfy \(D_{jj}\geq\eta_j\) and define the symmetric perturbation \(E=LDL^{\mathsf T}-P^{\mathsf T}AP\). Thus the factors represent the modified matrix \(P^{\mathsf T}AP+E\), not necessarily the original matrix.

Small-Pivot Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal regularization policy for small Cholesky pivots in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a symmetric matrix \(A\), permutation \(P\), pivot threshold \(\tau>0\), and initial shift \(\delta_0>0\). Attempt Cholesky factorization of \(P^{T}(A+\delta I)P\), initially with \(\delta=0\). If a computed squared pivot \(d_j\) satisfies \(d_j\le \tau s_j\), where \(s_j>0\) is a chosen local scale, abort the attempt, choose \(\delta\ge\delta_0\), increase \(\delta\) geometrically, and restart until every pivot passes the test or a shift limit is reached. Return the factor and applied shift, or report failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detect an inadequately positive Cholesky pivot, increase a diagonal shift, and refactor until pivots pass the scaled threshold or a limit is reached.
assumptions_latex: A finite maximum shift or restart count is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On success, \(P^{T}(A+\delta I)P=LL^{T}\) and \(d_j>\tau s_j\) for every \(j\).
review_flags: threshold and shift policy are implementation-dependent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to interpreting a small positive Cholesky pivot as a certificate of singularity or indefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the matrix \(B_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\) is symmetric positive definite and has Cholesky factor \(L_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\sqrt{\varepsilon})\). Its second squared pivot is \(\varepsilon\), which can be arbitrarily small. Thus smallness of a positive pivot, without a scale and error analysis, does not certify singularity or indefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SPD matrix diag(1, epsilon) has an arbitrarily small positive Cholesky pivot, so pivot smallness alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.title: Small Positive Pivot Is Inconclusive
Cholesky Breakdown Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic interpretation of a nonpositive or unusably small Cholesky pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: During exact Cholesky elimination of a symmetric matrix \(B\), the next squared pivot is the leading diagonal entry of the current Schur complement. If \(B\succ0\), every such value is strictly positive. Hence an exact-arithmetic value \(d_j\le0\) certifies that \(B\) is not positive definite. In floating-point arithmetic, a computed value \(\widehat d_j\le\tau s_j\) is instead a breakdown signal: it may indicate indefiniteness, singularity, severe ill-conditioning, or accumulated rounding error, but alone does not certify which cause occurred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpositive exact pivot disproves positive definiteness; a tiny computed pivot is only a numerical warning requiring further diagnosis.
assumptions_latex: Elimination has reached column \(j\) without an earlier exact zero divisor.
For the certificate, arithmetic is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_j\le0\Rightarrow B\not\succ0\); in floating point, \(\widehat d_j\le\tau s_j\) is diagnostic rather than conclusive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inertia preservation in a successful symmetric-indefinite LDL factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P^{\mathsf T}KP=LDL^{\mathsf T}\) with nonsingular \(L\), Sylvester's law of inertia gives \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)\). The numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of \(K\) are therefore obtained by summing the inertias of the scalar and two-by-two diagonal blocks of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A successful block LDL factorization reveals the matrix inertia through its diagonal pivot blocks.

Sparse LDL Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permuted sparse symmetric-indefinite factorization with scalar and block pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real symmetric matrix \(K\), a successful symmetric-indefinite elimination with nonsingular accepted pivots produces a permutation matrix \(P\), a unit lower-triangular sparse matrix \(L\), and a block-diagonal matrix \(D\) such that \(P^{T}KP=LDL^{T}\). Each diagonal block of \(D\) is either a nonsingular \(1\times1\) pivot or a nonsingular symmetric \(2\times2\) pivot. The stored pattern of \(L\) contains the fill generated by the ordering and any dynamic pivot interchanges. Linear systems are solved by applying \(P\), two triangular substitutions, and independent solves with the blocks of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric-indefinite elimination represents a permuted matrix as a unit triangular factor, scalar-or-block diagonal pivots, and the transposed factor.
assumptions_latex: \(K=K^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).
Every selected \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) pivot block is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{T}KP=LDL^{T}\), with \(D\) block diagonal in blocks of order one or two.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure-preserving alternative to unrestricted dynamic symmetric pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Static symmetric pivoting fixes, or severely restricts changes to, a permutation chosen from sparsity, scaling, or matching information before numerical elimination. It preserves the predicted symbolic structure more closely than unrestricted dynamic pivoting. If the prescribed scalar or block candidate fails the numerical acceptance test, the method must delay it, regularize it, enlarge the candidate set, or report failure; the fixed order alone gives no general numerical-stability guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static pivoting preserves a predicted sparse order but needs delay, regularization, or failure handling when its prescribed pivots are unacceptable.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each stage, inspect the current leading column and the comparison columns prescribed by the chosen Bunch-Kaufman variant. Accept a diagonal \(1\times1\) pivot when its magnitude satisfies the variant's threshold relative to relevant off-diagonal entries; otherwise symmetrically interchange a candidate index into position and accept either its diagonal entry or an admissible nonsingular \(2\times2\) block. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symbolic ordering predicts fill for a fixed elimination order, whereas threshold or rook pivoting may interchange or delay variables according to numerical values. Dynamic choices can introduce fill absent from the fixed-order prediction. Restricting candidates preserves more symbolic structure but can exhaust numerically acceptable pivots; enlarging the candidate region improves pivot availability at the cost of additional search and potentially greater fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic symmetric pivoting trades adherence to a sparse symbolic order against numerical pivot availability.

Symmetric Pivoting Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-based symmetric selection of scalar or two-by-two LDL pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a symmetric active matrix \(S\) and threshold \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). At each step, inspect a candidate diagonal entry and the largest relevant off-diagonal magnitude. Accept a \(1\times1\) pivot only when its diagonal magnitude meets the prescribed threshold relative to those entries; otherwise interchange rows and matching columns to test another diagonal candidate or select a nonsingular symmetric \(2\times2\) pivot block satisfying the block stability test. Apply the corresponding symmetric permutation, form the Schur-complement update, and continue. Output \(P,L,D\), together with any delayed or rejected pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose stable scalar or two-by-two pivots using threshold tests, always applying identical row and column interchanges to preserve symmetry.
assumptions_latex: An accepted pivot block is nonsingular under the implementation's stability test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every update preserves symmetry and yields the partial relation \(P^{T}KP=LDL^{T}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Use and limitation of comparing computed and theoretical inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When a matrix formulation predicts inertia \((n_+,n_-,n_0)\), a completed \(LDL^T\) factorization is inertia-consistent exactly when the signs of the eigenvalues of its pivot blocks total those counts. A mismatch detects failure of at least one assembly, model, factorization, or sign-classification assumption; a match alone does not bound backward error or conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare pivot-block sign counts with the formulation's expected inertia; disagreement is diagnostic, while agreement is not an accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Inertia Consistency Check
Factor Inertia Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inertia certification from a completed symmetric LDL factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a real symmetric matrix \(K\) has a computed factorization \(P^{T}KP=LDL^{T}\), where \(P\) is a permutation, \(L\) is nonsingular, and \(D\) is symmetric block diagonal. In exact arithmetic, congruence preserves inertia, so the numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of \(K\) equal the corresponding totals over the \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) blocks of \(D\). Thus block eigenvalue signs provide a directly checkable inertia certificate. In floating point, blocks near the sign tolerance must be reported as numerically ambiguous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count signs of the scalar and two-by-two pivot-block eigenvalues to recover the matrix inertia; near-zero blocks remain numerically ambiguous.

children.title: Pivot Magnitude Diagnostics

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon\ll1\), let \(K_\varepsilon=\begin{bmatrix}\varepsilon&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). The first scalar pivot in the displayed order is \(\varepsilon\) and produces multiplier \(1/\varepsilon\), yet both singular values of \(K_\varepsilon\) tend to \(1\) as \(\varepsilon\to0\), so \(\kappa_2(K_\varepsilon)\to1\). Thus a tiny local pivot can diagnose a poor pivot order without diagnosing global ill-conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny pivot may reflect a poor elimination order even when the full matrix is well conditioned.

Hence \(\max_i|\ell_i|=\max_i|a_i|/|d|\); a pivot small relative to its active column permits large multipliers and possible element growth.

Given thresholds \(0<\tau_{\mathrm{fail}}<\tau_{\mathrm{warn}}\), classify the pivot as acceptable when \(\rho_b\ge\tau_{\mathrm{warn}}\), small when \(\tau_{\mathrm{fail}}<\rho_b<\tau_{\mathrm{warn}}\), and numerically singular when \(\rho_b\le\tau_{\mathrm{fail}}\). For a scalar pivot, \(\sigma_{\min}(D_b)=|D_b|\); for a \(2\times2\) pivot it is the smaller singular value. The diagnostic is scale-dependent and is not, by itself, a condition-number estimate for the full matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If exact arithmetic produces \(P^TKP=LDL^T\) with permutation \(P\) and nonsingular \(L\), then \(K\) is singular if and only if the block-diagonal matrix \(D\) is singular. Equivalently, at least one scalar or two-by-two diagonal block of \(D\) has a zero eigenvalue. This conclusion concerns a completed factorization, not rejection of one candidate pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a completed exact LDL factorization with nonsingular L, singularity of D is equivalent to singularity of the original matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Completed-LDL Exact Singularity Certificate

assumptions_latex: A fixed induced norm, condition estimator, and warning threshold \(\tau>0\) are declared.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-invariant warning based on estimated proximity to singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonsingular \(K\), define \(\operatorname{rcond}(K)=1/(\|K\|\,\|K^{-1}\|)\) in a fixed induced norm. An estimate \(\widehat{\operatorname{rcond}}(K)\le\tau\) is a scale-invariant warning that perturbations small relative to the chosen norm scale may make the system effectively singular. It is not an exact rank certificate because the estimate and threshold are finite-precision quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A very small reciprocal condition estimate is a scale-invariant numerical-singularity warning, not proof of exact rank loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal-Condition Singularity Signal
Numerical Singularity Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined failure signals from a symmetric-indefinite direct factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P^{T}KP=LDL^{T}\) be attempted in floating point. Declare numerical singularity suspected, rather than mathematically proved, when an accepted pivot block has \(\sigma_{\min}(D_b)\le\tau s_b\), no admissible pivot can be found after permitted delays, or triangular solution produces a normwise relative residual exceeding a prescribed tolerance. Exact singularity is certified only if exact elimination produces a zero pivot block, equivalently a singular Schur complement at that stage. Tiny computed pivots, excessive growth, and large residuals may also result from scaling or severe ill-conditioning and therefore require corroborating checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tiny pivot blocks, exhausted pivot searches, or large solve residuals signal numerical singularity, but only an exact zero pivot certifies singularity.
assumptions_latex: Positive scaling and diagnostic tolerances are fixed.
The reported residual uses the original unpermuted system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\min}(D_b)\le\tau s_b\) or pivot-search failure is a warning; an exact zero pivot block certifies singularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a factorization of nonsingular \(S\), compute \(W=S^{-1}U\) and factor \(G=I_r+U^{\mathsf T}W\). For any \(b\), solve \(Sy=b\), \(Gz=U^{\mathsf T}y\), and set \(x=y-Wz\). Then \((S+UU^{\mathsf T})x=b\). The order-\(m\) factorization is confined to the chosen sparse core, while the correction factorization has order \(r\).

\(G=I_r+U^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}U\) is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central matrix-inversion identity for a sparse invertible core and dense low-rank correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular and \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\). Define \(G=I_r+U^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}U\) and \(H=S+UU^{\mathsf T}\). Then \(H\) is nonsingular if and only if \(G\) is nonsingular. In that case, \[H^{-1}=S^{-1}-S^{-1}UG^{-1}U^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Woodbury identity replaces inversion of the updated matrix by sparse-core solves and an r-dimensional correction, with equivalent nonsingularity conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is nonsingular.

Factor reuse is valid because the iterate-dependent coefficient matrix is unchanged while the centering and second-order correction alter only the right-hand side.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-correction refinement of a computed barrier-system solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonsingular matrix \(K\), right-hand side \(b\), an initial approximation \(x^{(0)}\), and reusable approximate factors of \(K\), repeat for \(j=0,1,\ldots\): compute \(r^{(j)}=b-Kx^{(j)}\) in residual precision, approximately solve \(K d^{(j)}=r^{(j)}\) using the factors, and set \(x^{(j+1)}=x^{(j)}+d^{(j)}\). Stop when \(\lVert r^{(j)}\rVert\leq\eta(\lVert K\rVert\lVert x^{(j)}\rVert+\lVert b\rVert)\), or when a prescribed iteration limit is reached, and return the last iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Refinement-Step Work and Geometric Step Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work accounting under a contracting fixed-factor refinement model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: One refinement correction requires one explicit residual evaluation, one application of the stored solve operator \(B\), and one vector update. Under \(\|I-BK\|\le q<1\), reducing the forward-error bound by a factor \(\theta\in(0,1)\) is guaranteed after at most \[k=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\theta)}{\log(1/q)}\right\rceil\] corrections. The additional work is therefore \(k\) residual evaluations, \(k\) factor solves, and \(k\) vector updates, excluding the original factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each refinement step costs a residual evaluation, a reused-factor solve, and an update; contraction gives a logarithmic correction count.
assumptions_latex: The correction operator is reused without rebuilding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left\lceil\log(1/\theta)/\log(1/q)\right\rceil\) corrections suffice.

notation.meaning: Requested reduction factor for the initial forward-error bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Refinement-Step Work and Geometric Step Count

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence boundary when residual evaluation, correction solves, or updates introduce bounded errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a refinement implementation satisfies \[e^{(j+1)}=(I-BK)e^{(j)}+f^{(j)},\qquad \|I-BK\|\le q<1,\qquad \|f^{(j)}\|\le\gamma.\] Then \[\|e^{(j)}\|\le q^j\|e^{(0)}\|+\frac{1-q^j}{1-q}\gamma.\] Thus bounded residual, correction-solve, and update errors generally limit refinement to an error neighborhood of radius at most \(\gamma/(1-q)\); they do not guarantee convergence to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite residual and update errors impose an accuracy floor even when the ideal refinement operator is contractive.
assumptions_latex: The aggregate perturbation obeys \(\|f^{(j)}\|\le\gamma\) at every correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}\|e^{(j)}\|\le\gamma/(1-q)\).

notation.meaning: Aggregate error from residual evaluation, correction solve, and update at step j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic contraction criterion for refinement using a fixed approximate inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be nonsingular and let a fixed linear correction operator \(B\) be used in \(x^{(j+1)}=x^{(j)}+B(b-Kx^{(j)})\). If \(x^*=K^{-1}b\) and \(e^{(j)}=x^*-x^{(j)}\), then \(e^{(j+1)}=(I-BK)e^{(j)}\). Hence, for any subordinate norm satisfying \(q:=\|I-BK\|<1\), \(\|e^{(j)}\|\le q^j\|e^{(0)}\|\). If no contraction condition holds, improvement is not guaranteed; for example, \(B=0\) leaves every iterate unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-operator refinement converges geometrically when its error-propagation matrix is a contraction; without contraction it can stagnate.

The correction operation is the fixed linear map \(B\).

Linear-Solve Residual Recalculation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise backward-error certificate formed from an explicitly recomputed residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a computed solution \(\widehat{x}\) of \(Kx=b\), recompute \(r=b-K\widehat{x}\) directly. For a vector norm and its subordinate matrix norm, define \[\beta(\widehat{x})=\frac{\lVert r\rVert}{\lVert K\rVert\lVert\widehat{x}\rVert+\lVert b\rVert},\] with \(\beta(\widehat{x})=0\) if the numerator and denominator both vanish. If \(\beta(\widehat{x})\leq\eta\), then there exist perturbations \(\Delta K\) and \(\Delta b\) satisfying \(\lVert\Delta K\rVert\leq\eta\lVert K\rVert\), \(\lVert\Delta b\rVert\leq\eta\lVert b\rVert\), and \((K+\Delta K)\widehat{x}=b+\Delta b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directly recomputed residual certifies that the computed solution exactly solves a nearby system whose matrix and right-hand side have normwise relative perturbations bounded by the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}\), \(b,\widehat{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}\)
The matrix norm is subordinate to the chosen vector norm.
\(r=b-K\widehat{x}\) is explicitly recomputed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta(\widehat{x})\leq\eta\) implies the stated normwise relative perturbation bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Backward Error from a Recomputed Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise alternative to the seed's normwise residual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r=b-K\widehat{x}\), let \(d=|K||\widehat{x}|+|b|\), with absolute values and products interpreted componentwise, and define \[\omega(\widehat{x})=\max_i\omega_i,\qquad \omega_i=\begin{cases}|r_i|/d_i,&d_i>0,\\0,&d_i=0\text{ and }r_i=0,\\+\infty,&d_i=0\text{ and }r_i\ne0.\end{cases}\] Then \(\omega(\widehat{x})\) is the least \(\varepsilon\ge0\) for which there exist perturbations satisfying \(|\Delta K|\le\varepsilon|K|\), \(|\Delta b|\le\varepsilon|b|\), and \((K+\Delta K)\widehat{x}=b+\Delta b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling each residual component by its rowwise attainable perturbation gives the exact componentwise relative backward error.
assumptions_latex: \(r=b-K\widehat{x}\) is explicitly recomputed.
Absolute values and inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(\widehat{x})=\min\{\varepsilon:\exists\Delta K,\Delta b,\ |\Delta K|\le\varepsilon|K|,\ |\Delta b|\le\varepsilon|b|,\ (K+\Delta K)\widehat{x}=b+\Delta b\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Backward Error from a Recomputed Residual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correction required when the explicitly calculated residual is itself affected by bounded rounding error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the calculated residual be \(\widetilde r=r+\delta r\), where \(r=b-K\widehat{x}\) and \(\|\delta r\|\le\rho\). For \(D=\|K\|\|\widehat{x}\|+\|b\|>0\), the true normwise backward error satisfies \[\beta(\widehat{x})\le\frac{\|\widetilde r\|+\rho}{D}.\] Consequently, testing only \(\|\widetilde r\|/D\le\eta\) is not a justified certificate unless residual-evaluation error is negligible or is included in the acceptance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calculated residual certifies backward error only after accounting for the error incurred while evaluating that residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde r=r+\delta r\).
\(\|\delta r\|\le\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta(\widehat{x})\le(\|\widetilde r\|+\rho)/D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Normal-Equation Iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility boundary for conjugate-gradient iteration on singular barrier normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=ADA^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), where \(D\succ0\) is diagonal and \(A\) is rank deficient. The equation \(Hy=b\) is consistent exactly when \(b\in\mathcal{R}(H)=\mathcal{R}(A)\), equivalently when \(b\perp\mathcal{N}(A^{\mathsf T})\). In exact arithmetic, conjugate gradients applied with \(y_0\in\mathcal{R}(H)\) to a compatible right-hand side remains in \(\mathcal{R}(H)\) and can recover the minimum-norm solution. If \(b\notin\mathcal{R}(H)\), no zero-residual solution exists, so an unmodified residual-based conjugate-gradient stopping rule cannot certify solution of the normal equations; projection, regularization, or a least-squares formulation is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular normal equations support CG only for compatible right-hand sides; incompatible null-space components require projection, regularization, or least-squares treatment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Range-Space Formulation of Singular Normal Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected SPD formulation and regularized limit for a compatible singular barrier normal equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H=ADA^{\mathsf T}\succeq0 with D\succ0. For b\in\mathcal R(H), the restriction H|_{\mathcal R(H)} is positive definite, and the unique solution in \mathcal R(H) is H^\dagger b. CG initialized in \mathcal R(H) remains in that subspace and is ordinary CG on the restricted operator. Moreover, (H+\delta I)^{-1}b\to H^\dagger b as \delta\downarrow0. If b has a nonzero component in \mathcal N(H), no zero-residual solution exists and the shifted solution's null-space component grows as 1/\delta.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible singular normal equation is SPD on its range; projected CG finds its minimum-norm solution, while incompatible null-space components prevent a zero residual.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: MINRES applied to a symmetric augmented primal-dual Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=K^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}\) be a nonsingular augmented barrier matrix, possibly indefinite, let \(r_0=b-Kx_0\), and set \(\beta=\lVert r_0\rVert_2\). Lanczos iteration constructs an orthonormal basis \(V_k\) of \(\mathcal{K}_k(K,r_0)\) and a tridiagonal relation \(KV_k=V_{k+1}\underline{T}_k\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(z_k\) minimizing \(\lVert\beta e_1-\underline{T}_kz\rVert_2\), set \(x_k=x_0+V_kz_k\), and stop when \(\lVert b-Kx_k\rVert_2\leq\eta\lVert b\rVert_2\). Consequently, \(x_k\) minimizes the residual norm over \(x_0+\mathcal{K}_k(K,r_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MINRES uses a Lanczos basis to minimize the residual over successive Krylov spaces of a symmetric indefinite barrier system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure-preservation condition for Krylov solution of augmented barrier systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the augmented barrier system \(Kx=b\) with \(K=K^{\mathsf T}\) indefinite. A preconditioned short-recurrence symmetric Krylov method is applicable when the preconditioner \(M\) is symmetric positive definite and is applied through the congruently transformed system \[M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}u=M^{-1/2}b,\qquad x=M^{-1/2}u.\] The transformed operator is symmetric in the Euclidean inner product, equivalently \(M^{-1}K\) is self-adjoint in the \(M\)-inner product. A nonsymmetric or indefinite preconditioner generally destroys this condition and invalidates the standard MINRES recurrence and residual-minimization guarantee.

Factorization-Based Preconditioners
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incomplete-factorization preconditioning for barrier normal or augmented systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) denote a barrier linear-system matrix. A factorization-based preconditioner replaces \(K\) by an efficiently solvable approximation \(M\): for a positive-definite normal equation, take \(M=\widetilde{L}\widetilde{L}^{\mathsf T}\succ0\); for a symmetric augmented system, use an appropriate symmetry-preserving approximate block factorization. The preconditioned operator is \(M^{-1}K\), and applying it requires one multiplication by \(K\) and triangular or block solves with the stored factors of \(M\). If \(K\succ0\), \(M\succ0\), and \(cM\preceq K\preceq CM\), then every eigenvalue of \(M^{-1}K\) lies in \([c,C]\) and its spectral condition number is at most \(C/c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate sparse factors define a cheaply invertible preconditioner; spectral equivalence bounds the eigenvalues and condition number of the preconditioned system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint preconditioning for primal-dual augmented Newton systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be positive diagonal, and define the augmented Newton matrix \(K=\begin{bmatrix}-D&A^{T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\). A constraint preconditioner is a readily invertible matrix \(P_C=\begin{bmatrix}-E&A^{T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\), where \(E\succ0\) approximates \(D\). Application of \(P_C^{-1}\) preserves the constraint block \(A\Delta x=r_p\) exactly; hence, when the right-preconditioned iteration starts with a constraint-feasible residual, its corrections remain in the corresponding constraint null space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasidefinite inertia and approximation-quality boundary for a regularized KKT preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\begin{bmatrix}-D&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(P_{\rho,\delta}=\begin{bmatrix}-(D+\rho I)&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&\delta I\end{bmatrix}\), the Schur complement \(A(D+\rho I)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}+\delta I\) is positive definite for arbitrary \(A\). Hence \(P_{\rho,\delta}\) is nonsingular with \(m\) positive and \(n\) negative eigenvalues. Moreover, \(P_{\rho,\delta}-K=\operatorname{diag}(-\rho I,\delta I)\), so its spectral-norm perturbation is \(\max\{\rho,\delta\}\). Large shifts can therefore improve factorization robustness while degrading approximation quality; nonsingularity alone does not imply clustered eigenvalues of \(P_{\rho,\delta}^{-1}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive primal and dual shifts give a nonsingular quasidefinite preconditioner even for rank-deficient constraints, but large shifts can make it a poor approximation.

Regularization-Based Preconditioners
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized preconditioning of ill-conditioned barrier KKT systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the symmetric augmented system \(K\binom{u}{v}=b\), with \(K=\begin{bmatrix}-D&A^{T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(D\succ0\), a regularization-based preconditioner replaces the diagonal blocks by \(P_{\rho,\delta}=\begin{bmatrix}-(D+\rho I)&A^{T}\\A&\delta I\end{bmatrix}\), where \(\rho>0\) and \(\delta>0\). The shifts make the primal block uniformly negative definite and the dual Schur complement \(A(D+\rho I)^{-1}A^{T}+\delta I\) positive definite, including when \(A\) is rank deficient. The parameters should be small enough that \(P_{\rho,\delta}\) remains a useful approximation to \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive primal and dual shifts produce a nonsingular preconditioner and stabilize barrier systems whose scaling or constraint rank makes unregularized solves unreliable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant relative-residual rule for every inner Newton solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At outer iteration \(k\), let \(J_kd_k=-F_k\) be the Newton equation and let \(r_k=J_k\widehat d_k+F_k\) be the residual of an approximate inner solve. A fixed-inner-accuracy condition chooses one constant \(\eta\in[0,1)\), independent of \(k\), and accepts \(\widehat d_k\) when \[\|r_k\|\leq \eta\|F_k\|.\] If the inner method uses a preconditioned norm, the same norm must be used on both sides. The rule controls relative linearization error uniformly but does not tighten automatically as the barrier iteration approaches a solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Congruence Equilibration
Linear-System Equilibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal equilibration of a barrier Newton system before numerical factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a nonsingular Newton matrix \(K\), right-hand side \(r\), tolerance \(\tau>0\), and iteration limit \(L\), initialize positive diagonal matrices \(E_0=I\) and \(F_0=I\). For \(j=0,\ldots,L-1\), form \(K_j=E_jKF_j\), compute each nonzero row norm \(p_i=\|(K_j)_{i:}\|_2\) and column norm \(q_k=\|(K_j)_{:k}\|_2\), and update
\[E_{j+1}=\operatorname{diag}(p_i^{-1/2})E_j,\qquad F_{j+1}=F_j\operatorname{diag}(q_k^{-1/2}).\]
Stop when all computed norms lie in \([1-\tau,1+\tau]\), or after \(L\) iterations. Solve \((EKF)z=Er\) and return \(d=Fz\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteratively rescale rows and columns of the Newton matrix toward unit norm, solve the equilibrated system, and map the direction back.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\) is nonsingular and has no zero row or column.
Norms and diagonal scaling factors are representable in the working arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned vector \(d=Fz\) satisfies \(Kd=r\) in exact arithmetic whenever \((EKF)z=Er\).

Unscaled-Accuracy Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of scaled residuals and complementarity into original LP accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the scaling \(\widehat A=D_rAD_c\), \(\widehat b=D_rb\), \(\widehat c=D_cc\), with \(x=D_c\widehat x\), \(y=D_r\widehat y\), and \(s=D_c^{-1}\widehat s\), define scaled residuals
\[\widehat r_p=\widehat A\widehat x-\widehat b,\qquad \widehat r_d=\widehat A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y+\widehat s-\widehat c.\]
The original residuals obey
\[r_p=D_r^{-1}\widehat r_p,\qquad r_d=D_c^{-1}\widehat r_d,\qquad x^{\mathsf T}s=\widehat x^{\mathsf T}\widehat s.\]
Consequently, scaled stopping tolerances certify original-space accuracy only after applying the inverse scaling and normalizing against the original data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled residuals must be mapped through inverse scaling before reporting original-model feasibility; complementarity is invariant under the paired variable scaling.

Primal Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-variable regularization of the reduced primal-dual Newton equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta=XS^{-1}\succ0\) be the barrier scaling and let \(r_x\) and \(r_y\) denote the reduced Newton right-hand sides. For \(\rho>0\), primal regularization replaces the augmented system by
\[\begin{pmatrix}-(\Theta^{-1}+\rho I)&A^{\mathsf T}\\ A&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\ \Delta y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}r_x\\ r_y\end{pmatrix}.\]
Equivalently, after eliminating \(\Delta x\), the multiplier equation has coefficient
\[A(\Theta^{-1}+\rho I)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}.\]
The positive shift bounds the inverse primal block even when entries of \(\Theta^{-1}\) are very small; the resulting direction solves a perturbed, rather than exact, Newton equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a positive shift to the primal block controls extreme barrier scaling but introduces a deliberate perturbation of the Newton equations.

Dual Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-block regularization of the reduced primal-dual Newton equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta=XS^{-1}\succ0\). For \(\delta>0\), dual regularization uses
\[\begin{pmatrix}-\Theta^{-1}&A^{\mathsf T}\\ A&\delta I\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\ \Delta y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}r_x\\ r_y\end{pmatrix}.\]
Eliminating \(\Delta x\) gives
\[(A\Theta A^{\mathsf T}+\delta I)\Delta y=r_y+A\Theta r_x.\]
Hence every eigenvalue of the normal-equation coefficient is at least \(\delta\), including when \(A\) is row-rank deficient. The regularization perturbs the linearized primal-feasibility equation by \(\delta\Delta y\), so residuals must ultimately be assessed against the unregularized equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive shift in the multiplier block makes the normal equations positive definite, even with dependent constraints, but perturbs primal feasibility.

Coupled Primal-Dual Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous regularization of primal and multiplier blocks in a barrier Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\Theta=XS^{-1}\succ0\), \(\rho>0\), and \(\delta>0\), the coupled regularized system is
\[\begin{pmatrix}-(\Theta^{-1}+\rho I)&A^{\mathsf T}\\ A&\delta I\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\ \Delta y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}r_x\\ r_y\end{pmatrix}.\]
Writing \(M=\Theta^{-1}+\rho I\), elimination yields
\[(AM^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}+\delta I)\Delta y=r_y+AM^{-1}r_x.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized controller for adapting regularization using factorization diagnostics and the original Newton residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain regularization parameters \((\rho,\delta)\) within prescribed positive lower and upper bounds. On each of at most \(J\) attempts, solve the corresponding regularized system. Reject an attempt if its declared factorization diagnostic fails or if \[\eta(d):=\frac{\|b-Kd\|}{\|K\|\|d\|+\|b\|}>\eta_{\mathrm{acc}}.\] After rejection, multiply active parameters by \(\gamma>1\), capped at their upper bounds. Accept only when both tests pass. After acceptance with \(\eta(d)\le\eta_{\mathrm{good}}<\eta_{\mathrm{acc}}\), parameters for the next outer iteration may be divided by \(\gamma\), floored at their lower bounds. If the attempt limit or parameter bounds are exhausted without acceptance, return failure and no direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase bounded regularization after failed diagnostics, decrease it after comfortably accurate solves, and accept only against the original Newton equation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given initial parameters \(\rho_0,	6\delta_0>0\), bounds \(\rho_{\min},\delta_{\min}>0\), growth factor \(\gamma>1\), and acceptance tolerance \(\eta\), attempt the coupled regularized Newton solve at iteration \(k\). \[(\rho_k,\delta_k)\leftarrow(\gamma\rho_k,\gamma\delta_k)\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact row dependence and its effect on barrier normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For equality constraints \(Ax=b\) with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the constraints are linearly dependent exactly when
\[\operatorname{rank}(A)<m,\]
equivalently, when there exists \(0\ne u\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}u=0\). The equality system is consistent only if every such vector also satisfies \(u^{\mathsf T}b=0\). For every positive diagonal \(\Theta\), dependence implies
\[u^{\mathsf T}A\Theta A^{\mathsf T}u=0,\]
so the unregularized barrier normal-equation matrix \(A\Theta A^{\mathsf T}\) is singular.
